statement: Prefer short, clear sentences; each carries one claim and ideally one causal or logical step; split a sentence that is hard to follow. One sentence holds one role: never a premise, a cause and end-point values together; split it so each holds one.
why: A reader holds one step at a time.
good: The skew moves the slot harmonic away from the resonance. This lowers the noise.
bad: The skew, which moves the slot harmonic, lowers the noise and changes the torque.
provenance: writing-style rule 1; examples paraphrase; original withheld until publication; user review 2026-11-23 P2-G1 (absorbs sentence.one-role)

statement: Never bundle a parenthetical definition with its consequence; the definition gets its own sentence and the consequence follows in the next.
why: A definition and a consequence are two steps.
provenance: writing-style rule 1; self-check

statement: A sentence stays within dimension sentence.max-words; split a longer one at a logical link. Every sentence is short enough to read aloud in one breath.
why: Long sentences hide their logic.
provenance: old lint 'length'; self-check (one breath); user ruling 2026-11-22 (about 35 words)

statement: Short sentences are fine, but a run of very short sentences (below dimension sentence.min-words, at least dimension sentence.short-run in a row), each carrying one bare fact, reads machine-written; merge or connect them.
why: Bare facts in a row lose their links.
bad: These changes reverse. The loss falls.
provenance: old lint 'bare'; user ruling 2026-11-22 (sentence length and linkage)

statement: Avoid ornate or showy phrasing; prefer everyday verbs and concrete nouns over abstract noun-heavy constructions; no showy adjectives, unquantified intensifiers or abstract-noun piles.
why: Showy wording claims importance instead of showing it.
bad: has placed X at the centre of; a focal point of intense development; remarkable; decisive leap
provenance: writing-style rule 2; self-check; field habits (rule 2)

statement: Use one canonical term per concept throughout the document, fixed at the start (e.g. in the nomenclature); never substitute synonyms for variety; qualify a term only where the contrast matters, and then consistently. One concept, one name: introduce a qualified term once, then use only the short name.
why: Synonyms make the reader ask whether two things differ.
provenance: writing-style rule 4; user ruling 2026-11-10; self-check; user review 2026-11-23 P4-budget: checked by lint

statement: State goals and trends as trends ("continues to rise"), never in an obligation voice ("must deliver").
why: The obligation voice reads as a command.
good: The power density of traction machines continues to rise.
bad: Traction machines must deliver a higher power density.
provenance: writing-style rule 6; user review 2026-11-23 C1 (new non-personified example; the old example "motors are pursuing higher efficiency" conflicted with wording.no-human-action)

statement: Organise paragraphs as one line of reasoning toward the gap and the solution; no total-part scaffolding for unordered categories; numbered steps only when order is part of the method; an introduction reads as one narrative line, not an annotated survey; no numbered contribution lists.
why: Scaffolding replaces reasoning with a list.
bad: X can be grouped into N strands. The first strand is ...
provenance: writing-style rule 7; self-check; fields README shared practice 1

statement: Introduce background only where the main line needs it and only in the detail it needs; no technology overviews unless used later.
why: Unused background dilutes the gap.
provenance: writing-style rule 8

statement: Every sentence hooks onto its predecessor (shared term, anaphora, causal connective) and follows from it; if a reader cannot say why it comes next, add the link. A list of properties becomes a mechanism chain, one step per sentence. Each paragraph opens with a link to the previous one. A bare assertion that hooks onto nothing is folded into the causal sentence it supports.
why: Unlinked sentences read as a list.
good: X raises A. Higher A lowers B and hence improves C.
provenance: writing-style rules 10, 22; user ruling 2026-11-22 (every sentence links); self-check; user review 2026-11-23 P2-G1 (absorbs sentence.no-bare-assertion)

statement: Old information opens each sentence (the concept the previous sentence ended on, or the actor whose story it continues) and the fact the reader should remember closes it, not a qualifier, condition or operating detail; the frame (quantity, plane, condition) comes before the item it frames, within a sentence and within a paragraph.
why: The reader links old to new and remembers what the sentence ends on.
good: ... raises the bearing current. This current erodes the races.
bad: ... raises the bearing current. Race erosion grows with the bearing current.
provenance: merged 2026-11-23 P2-G2 from cohesion.topic-position, sentence.stress-position, cohesion.context-before-new; P3 (S3 Gopen and Swan); examples paraphrase; original withheld until publication; P2 (S3); examples paraphrase; original withheld until publication

statement: Every paragraph runs context, content, conclusion: the first sentence sets the question and the last states the answer as one causal sentence drawn from its facts, not a list of expectations or levers; a section closes the same way.
why: A results paragraph without its answer is incomplete.
good: ends on "Hence the second carrier group carries most of the magnet loss."
bad: ends on "Fig. 5 shows the spectra."
provenance: P6 (S2); absorbs structure.causal-close (writing-style rule 25) 2026-11-23 P2-G2

statement: Treat each topic in one place, in one contiguous passage (no zig-zag); genuinely parallel items in one list take parallel form. Elsewhere cite its section, equation, figure or table and state only the conclusion the current argument needs; restate only to add a qualification or change scope.
why: One topic in one place keeps one source of truth in the text; a cross-reference advances the reasoning rather than restarting it.
provenance: P7 (S2); writing-style rule 9; self-check; merged from structure.one-topic-one-place, argument.cross-reference-no-restatement (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G3)

statement: Fix one central message before drafting; the title states it and every section is checked against it.
why: One message keeps the paper coherent.
good: Bearing currents set the insulation life of inverter-fed fan motors.
bad: Analysis of losses in a fan motor.

statement: Results subsection headings follow dimension heading.style: declarative states the finding ("Rotor skew lowers the cogging torque"), topic names the subject ("Cogging torque versus rotor skew"); one style throughout.
why: Headings of one style let the reader scan the results.
provenance: P9 (S2), heading part; user review 2026-11-23 C12 (a dimension, not a fixed rule); renamed from structure.results-heading-style (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G3)

statement: No result appears before the gap sentence; the closing sentence returns to broad relevance (broad-narrow-broad).
why: Results need the gap to matter.

statement: The introduction never repeats abstract sentences. When dimension format.short is yes (digest, letter, extended abstract), the introduction may skip what the abstract already says (context, gap, purpose) and start at the first point the body needs; this never removes a definition the body needs.
why: Repetition wastes the page budget of a short format.
provenance: P20 (S1, S4); writing-style rule 43; user ruling 2026-11-22 (digest introduction); user review 2026-11-23 C10/C14 (split; tied to the venue dimension format.short). The conclusion half is criterion structure.conclusion-not-abstract-copy.

statement: No "novel", "analysis of", "study on" in a title; use specific descriptors.
why: Generic words carry no information.

statement: The introduction states mechanisms, directions and relative sizes only; the abstract and conclusion do so too unless dimension numbers.abstract-conclusion says otherwise. Operating points, absolute values, fitted coefficients and point counts stay in the results. A number may appear in a general section when it is itself the transferable finding (exponent, ratio, bound), without its operating point.
why: Case values belong where the case is described.
good: PWM adds a large part of the loss.
bad: 1.67 kW at 450 N.m and 5000 r/min (in the introduction)
provenance: writing-style rule 15; user rulings 2026-11-08, 2026-11-12; self-check

statement: Use the term the field already uses (check a textbook or the cited papers); introduce a new term only for a new concept, define it once and say why no existing term fits; no acronyms for single-use concepts. Keep a type descriptor on the noun it qualifies. Plain wording is for general prose; a technical concept takes its correct domain term, never a lay paraphrase or a metaphor.
why: Coined terms make the reader translate; a misplaced descriptor changes the meaning.
good: first and second carrier groups; DC and AC copper loss; a hairpin winding with two three-phase sets
bad: carrier band and double-carrier band; conductor DC and conductor AC; two hairpin winding sets
provenance: writing-style rule 16; user ruling 2026-11-08; self-check; field weak patterns; writing-style rule 16; user ruling 2026-11-08; self-check; merged from terms.established-not-coined, terms.descriptor-on-noun (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G3); merged wording.technical-precision, wording.no-metaphor-term (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G4)

statement: The manuscript names itself as dimension self-reference says (either: "this paper" or the name of its format, such as "this digest"), never alternating with other names in subject position.
why: One name for the document.
good: This paper analyses ...
bad: This digest analyses ... This work shows ...
provenance: writing-style rule 17; user ruling 2026-11-08; self-check; renamed from style.self-reference (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G3)

statement: The abstract, introduction and conclusion open with the broadest shared context and narrow by one level per sentence (application, machine class, regime, problem) to the gap, then state what the paper does, finds and why it matters; never open on a technical specific. The conclusion opens with the question the paper answered. Give a specialty concept's role in plain words before, or instead of, its symbol or name.
why: Readers enter from shared context and may not know the symbol.
provenance: writing-style rule 18; user ruling 2026-11-08; self-check; writing-style rule 18; self-check; merged from structure.broad-to-narrow, abstract.role-before-symbol (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G3)

statement: One sentence carries one step; a semicolon in prose (outside maths) splits into separate sentences.
why: Semicolon chains hide steps.
provenance: writing-style rule 18; user review 2026-11-23 P2-G1 (lint, scope all)

statement: Write for a practitioner of the field who is not a specialist: name each specialty concept with its classic reference before use and state only the property the argument relies on; cite textbook material instead of re-deriving it; explain at length only what is specific to this paper, ordered familiar to special.
why: A tutorial background is a defect; an unexplained specialty term is a wall.
provenance: writing-style rule 19; user ruling 2026-11-09; self-check

statement: Do not nest clauses such as "a simulation in which ... so that ..."; split them into independent sentences.
why: Nesting hides the order of steps.
provenance: writing-style rule 22; user ruling 2026-11-10; old lint '22-nested'

statement: Do not open a sentence with a noun clause ("How ... is set by", "What has not been shown is"); give it a concrete subject.
why: A noun clause delays the subject.
bad: How the harmonic divides is set by ...
provenance: writing-style rule 22; user ruling 2026-11-10; old lint '22-nounclause'

statement: The subject names the physical cause, not a vague actor; the action sits in the main verb, with no nominalised subjects or objects carrying "occurs", "takes place", "is done" or "results in": name the physical quantity and give it a verb.
why: A vague subject or a nominalisation hides the mechanism and its actor.
good: the harmonic current depends on the high-frequency inductance; The shift reduces the harmonic.
bad: the machine itself sets the ripple current; A reduction of the harmonic occurs with the shift; The iron-loss rise agrees with ...
provenance: writing-style rule 22; user ruling 2026-11-10; merged sentence.action-in-verb (writing-style rule 36(e); P4 (S3); user ruling 2026-11-12); user review 2026-11-23 P4-budget

statement: Do not announce novelty or label the paper's work with an ill-fitting abstract noun; state what the paper does and finds, in order, and let the increment over cited work follow from it.
why: Announced novelty invites doubt.
bad: Its novelty is ..., not ...; attribution; to the best of our knowledge
provenance: writing-style rule 23; user ruling 2026-11-10; old lint '22-announce'; fields README shared practice 2

statement: The statement of purpose names the application.
why: The application frames the relevance.
good: ... for offshore wind generators
provenance: writing-style rule 23; user ruling 2026-11-10; example paraphrase; original withheld until publication

statement: The introduction carries a roadmap as dimension introduction.roadmap says: per-section closes the introduction with the purpose statement followed by one sentence per section stating its role (not its findings), repeating nothing; none omits it (short formats).
why: The roadmap orients; findings there duplicate.
provenance: writing-style rule 24; self-check; now follows dimension introduction.roadmap (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G3)

statement: Start a section with its first substantive fact linked to what the reader knows. A scope statement (what this study investigates: "In this paper, both angles are investigated ...") is allowed. A section-by-section preview ("Section II describes ...", "the rest of this paper is organised as follows", "as discussed below") is not; the roadmap lives only in the introduction (introduction.roadmap).
why: Previews delay content; a scope statement is content.
good: In this paper, the bearing currents of an inverter-fed pump motor are investigated at two cable lengths.
bad: Section III describes the model and Section IV discusses the results.
provenance: writing-style rule 25; user ruling 2026-11-10; self-check; user review 2026-11-23 C7 (scope statement allowed, section preview flagged by lint)

statement: Do not open with an abstract umbrella sentence; name the concrete quantities directly.
why: Umbrella sentences carry no fact.
bad: Each component is produced by the quantity that acts on it.
provenance: writing-style rule 25; user ruling 2026-11-10; self-check

statement: Never define a quantity circularly.
why: A circular definition explains nothing.
bad: inductance as flux over current, then current as flux over inductance
provenance: writing-style rule 25; user ruling 2026-11-10; self-check

statement: Use technical verbs, not personified or spoken ones: quantities do not see, feed, decide, go or link; avoid spoken phrases. Machines, methods, planes and quantities do not meet needs, pursue goals, need, seek, help or carry intentions; state the physical action.
why: Personified verbs hide the physics.
good: is limited by the leakage inductance
bad: sees the leakage inductance; case by case; well documented
provenance: writing-style rule 26; user ruling 2026-11-10; old lint '26-verb'; merged wording.no-human-action (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G4)

statement: No vague "there", "this split", "these studies": name the plane, quantity or works.
why: The reader must know what is meant.
provenance: writing-style rule 26; user ruling 2026-11-10; old lint '25-vague'

statement: Do not start consecutive sentences with the same pronoun ("Its ... Its ...").
why: A pronoun run reads mechanical.
provenance: writing-style rule 26; user ruling 2026-11-10; old lint '26-its'

statement: Describe prior work by what it covered: a single study's finding stays that study's finding ("a comparative study found ...") and is not generalised; never claim that prior work has not studied something.
why: One study is one data point, and absence claims are rarely provable.
good: Prior studies of X covered A and B [1], [2].
bad: X has not been examined.
provenance: merged 2026-11-23 P2-G2 from argument.single-study-scope (writing-style rule 26) and argument.no-absence-claim (user ruling 2026-11-17; field weak patterns (EMD, PED))

statement: Relative clauses follow dimension sentence.relative-clause: forbid flags ", which" tails and restrictive that/which/who/whose clauses on nouns (use an adjective, a prepositional phrase or a separate sentence); nonrestrictive-only flags the restrictive clauses and allows a short ", which" tail; allow flags neither.
why: Relative clauses pile facts on one noun.
provenance: writing-style rules 29, 41; user ruling 2026-11-22; old lint '29-tail' (which part); user review 2026-11-23 P2-G1 (merges sentence.which-tail and sentence.no-relative-on-noun)

statement: Do not hang a ", whose ..." clause or a ", computed/giving/resulting ..." participle on the end of a sentence; give the fact its own sentence with its real subject.
why: The real actor disappears in a tail.
good: Eddy currents in the laminations change this impedance.
bad: , computed from the field
provenance: writing-style rule 29; old lint '29-tail' (participle part)

statement: Mix sentence forms (subject-first, phrase-opened, short, long). An opening phrase is used where it carries the link; a decorative opener that only adds a comma is not; never more than dimension opener.max-run phrase-plus-comma openings in a row, and about one in three at most. Connective openers (phrase vocabulary, when opener) carry the link and do not count.
why: Decorative openers are noise.
good: As a result, ...; Therefore, ...
bad: In the steady state, ...; Grouped by m, ...
provenance: writing-style rule 33; user ruling 2026-11-12; old lint '33-openers'; self-check; user review 2026-11-23 C4 (no contrast connective as a common example)

statement: Do not join two contrasting facts in one sentence with "while", "although" or ", but". Give each fact its own sentence; set side by side, the two sentences carry the contrast, and no fixed connective is required. The words of dimension connective.avoid are flagged under this rule as well.
why: One sentence, one fact.
good: The frame noise rises with the load. The bearing noise falls with the load.
bad: The frame noise rises with the load, while the bearing noise falls.
provenance: writing-style rule 36(a); user ruling 2026-11-12; self-check; user review 2026-11-23 C4 (common recommends no fixed contrast connective); user review 2026-11-23 P2-G1 (absorbs author.no-however, author.no-whereas via connective.avoid)

statement: Word order: the verb follows the grammatical subject at once, with no phrase, appositive or long modifier between them (move it out or into its own sentence); a relative clause never inverts object and agent.
why: The reader waits for the verb.
good: Switching excitation raises the rotor magnet loss.
bad: the second, beyond its peak near M=0.6, grows
provenance: writing-style rule 36(b); P1 (S3); user ruling 2026-11-12; self-check; user review 2026-11-23 P2-G1 (absorbs sentence.no-inverted-relative)

statement: No mirrored sentence pairs built to one template; vary the structure or merge the content.
why: Templates read generated.
bad: X thus ... . Y, in contrast, ...
provenance: writing-style rule 36(d); user ruling 2026-11-12

statement: Never place a single comma between a subject and its verb.
why: A lone comma there is a grammar error.
good: The thermal network is used ...
bad: The thermal network, is used ...
provenance: new (corpus slip); examples paraphrase; original withheld until publication

statement: A compound subject ("A and B") takes a plural verb.
why: Agreement is grammar.
good: Skew and rotor shaping reduce ...
bad: Skew and rotor shaping ... reduces ...
provenance: new (corpus slip); examples paraphrase; original withheld until publication

statement: An opening participle phrase has the sentence subject as its actor.
why: A dangling modifier names the wrong actor.
good: Equation (1) gives the loss.
bad: Using (1), the loss was computed.
provenance: P17 (S1); grammar, hence common

statement: Hyphenate a compound modifier before its noun (hyphenate vocabulary).
why: An unhyphenated modifier misparses.
good: high-speed rotor; FEA-based model
bad: high speed rotor; FEA based model
provenance: new (corpus slips); examples paraphrase; original withheld until publication

statement: Fixed phrases and collocations take their standard form (forbidden and collocation vocabulary).
why: A broken fixed phrase is an error.
good: with regard to
bad: with regards to
provenance: new (corpus slip)

statement: No slash-joined word lists in prose; write them with "and" or "or". Units with a slash (r/min) are not lists.
why: A slash is ambiguous between and and or.
good: winding, iron and magnet losses
bad: winding/iron/magnet losses
provenance: new; extends table.one-quantity-per-cell to prose

statement: All prose and figure text (labels, legends, captions) follow dimension spelling.variant; bibliography titles and quotations keep their published spelling; LaTeX code (commands, environments, keys, labels, citation keys) keeps its spelling; words spelt alike in both variants stay.
why: One document, one spelling.
provenance: writing-style rule 40; user ruling 2026-11-22; old lint '40-english'

statement: In the source, start a new line after each sentence and after clause-separating commas in long sentences.
why: Clean diffs; the output is unaffected.
provenance: writing-style rule 11; self-check

statement: In the conclusion, what the paper did takes the tense of dimension conclusion.tense; findings that hold in general stay in the present.
why: One tense per role.
good: This paper has analysed ...
bad: This paper analysed ...
provenance: writing-style rule 46; user ruling 2026-11-22; old lint '46-tense'

statement: Tie every critique to a location in the manuscript (section, equation, table, figure) instead of vague critique.
why: A located point can be answered; a vague one cannot.
good: Section 3.2 states ...; Table 4 reports ...
bad: The method is unclear.
provenance: configs/templates/polish-checklist.md (Language), merged 2026-11-22

statement: Write review comments in the active voice, state each point directly without hedging, and address requests to the authors ("The authors should ...", "Please provide ...") rather than as bare imperatives.
why: Direct, addressed comments are actionable.
provenance: merged review-comment.active-voice, review-comment.no-hedging, review-comment.address-authors (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G4)

statement: The compiled manuscript stays within dimension document.page-limit (references inside or outside it per reference.inside-page-limit); past the limit, say so at once and offer a compensating cut.
why: A venue rejects an over-length submission.
provenance: check of process.page-budget-each-edit; the per-edit habit moved to skills/write (user review 2026-11-23 P2-G4)

statement: Where dimension numbers.abstract-conclusion is finding-then-value, state each finding first, as a mechanism or direction, then its value in the case examined ("<finding>, which is <value> in this case"); the value never precedes or replaces the finding. Where it is mechanisms-only, give no values.
why: The finding transfers; the value illustrates it.
good: Rotor skew lowers the cogging torque, which amounts to 0.8 N.m for the case examined.
provenance: author.abstract-finding-then-value (user ruling 2026-11-22; writing-style rule 42); user review 2026-11-23 P2-G7; example paraphrase; original withheld until publication

statement: Follow dimension conclusion.future-work: where future work is written, it closes the conclusion and names concrete conditions and components, not a promise of "experimental validation".
why: A named scope makes future work credible.
good: Future work extends the model to other ambient temperatures and load cycles and includes the bearing losses.
bad: will be studied in the future
provenance: author.conclusion-future-work (user ruling 2026-11-17, supervisor; field weak patterns EMD, PED); user review 2026-11-23 P2-G7 (not every paper); example paraphrase; original withheld until publication
